h1: UPS vs Solar vs Generator: Cost per Backup Hour Over Five Years
author: ali-ahmad

fields.name: load_w
fields.label: Load during a power cut
fields.hint: What runs together on backup: for example four fans, lights, a router and a TV. Add up the watts on the labels or use the home load calculator. Very large loads (a whole house with ACs) are beyond the UPS and generator sizes in our price list.

fields.name: surge_w
fields.label: Starting watts
fields.hint: Only if the backup runs a motor (water pump, fridge, AC): the load plus the biggest motor's extra starting watts. The UPS, generator and hybrid inverter must also start it, so each is sized for the larger of the load × margin and this. Leave blank for fans, lights and electronics.

fields.name: hours
fields.label: Power cut hours a day
fields.hint: Average loadshedding hours a day over the year in your area.

fields.name: years
fields.label: Years to compare
fields.hint: Five years covers one tubular battery replacement; try ten to see the long run.

fields.name: tariff
fields.label: Electricity rate
fields.hint: Energy rate of your slab, for the units a UPS takes from the grid to recharge. The default is the unprotected rate for 301 to 400 units a month.

fields.name: city
fields.label: City
fields.hint: Sets how many solar panels it takes to refill the battery on an average day.

fields.name: fuel_price
fields.label: Petrol price
fields.hint: Leave blank to use the latest petrol price in our data (dated under Sources), or type today's pump price.

fields.name: days
fields.label: Days with power cuts a month
fields.hint: Lower it if cuts happen only on some days.

UPS: {{out.ups_kva}} kVA, tubular batteries: {{out.batteries|int}} ({{out.bank_wh|int}} Wh needed), {{out.ups_buy|rs}}; recharge {{out.recharge_kwh_year|int}} units a year × {{out.tariff|rs2}} = {{out.ups_run_year|rs}}; battery replacements: {{out.ups_repl|int}}, {{out.ups_repl_rs|rs}}; charger check: {{out.refill_need_kwh|2}} kWh to put back in {{out.refill_hours|int}} grid hours, {{out.charger_a|int}} A at {{out.bank_v}} V gives up to {{out.refill_max_kwh|2}} kWh; total {{out.ups_total|rs}} ÷ {{out.backup_hours|int}} h = {{out.ups_per_hour|rs}}. Generator: {{out.gen_kva}} kVA, {{out.gen_buy|rs}}; {{out.l_per_h|2}} litres an hour × {{out.run_h_year|int}} h × {{out.fuel_price|rs2}} = {{out.fuel_year|rs}} fuel plus {{out.oil_year|rs}} oil a year; total {{out.gen_total|rs}} ÷ {{out.backup_hours|int}} h = {{out.gen_per_hour|rs}}. Hybrid solar: {{out.inverter_kw}} kW inverter, {{out.lithium_packs|int}} lithium pack(s), {{out.panels|int}} panels, {{out.solar_buy|rs}}; battery replacements: {{out.solar_repl|int}}, {{out.solar_repl_rs|rs}}; total {{out.solar_total|rs}} ÷ {{out.backup_hours|int}} h = {{out.solar_per_hour|rs}}.
key_facts: Cost per backup hour = (equipment + running cost a year × years + battery replacements) ÷ hours of backup over the same years; it puts a cheap-to-buy generator and a dear-to-buy solar system on one scale.

For {{in.load_w|int}} W through {{in.hours|int}} hours a day a petrol generator burns about {{out.l_per_h|2}} litres an hour, {{out.fuel_year|rs}} of petrol a year. Cheapest to buy here: {{out.cheapest_buy|raw}}; dearest after the first year (purchase plus one year of running): {{out.first_year_dearest|raw}}.

A UPS takes more units from the grid than it delivers: {{out.recharge_kwh_year|int}} units a year here, {{out.ups_run_year|rs}} at {{out.tariff|rs2}} a unit, and its tubular batteries are replaced every {{out.tubular_life_years|int}} years.

For a small load and short cuts: {{ex.1.in.load_w|int}} W for {{ex.1.in.hours|int}} hours a day costs {{ex.1.out.ups_per_hour|rs}} per backup hour on a UPS against {{ex.1.out.solar_per_hour|rs}} on hybrid solar, and the cheapest is {{ex.1.out.cheapest|raw}}; even a small solar backup buys a whole lithium pack and a hybrid inverter built for it.

formula.text: Cost per backup hour = (B + Y × R + N × P) ÷ (h × days × twelve × Y)
lines: B = equipment price (middle of the price range in our data, installation extra); Y = years compared
R = running cost a year: UPS recharge units × tariff; generator fuel (litres an hour × hours × price) + oil changes; hybrid solar none
N × P = battery replacements within the period × battery price (none in the final year of life)
Battery bank: UPS tubular Wh = load W × h ÷ (DoD × inverter efficiency); lithium kWh likewise, bought in whole packs
Generator litres an hour = no-load fuel × rated kW + fuel per kWh × load kW (the fuel calculator's curve)

sections.h2: Which is the cheapest backup for loadshedding?
p: With the defaults, {{in.load_w|int}} W for {{in.hours|int}} hours a day over {{in.years|int}} years, the answer is {{out.cheapest|raw}} at {{out.cheapest_total|rs}} in total. The UPS comes to {{out.ups_total|rs}}, hybrid solar to {{out.solar_total|rs}} and the generator to {{out.gen_total|rs}}; solar has no running cost once bought, the generator pays for petrol every hour.

The answer can change with the load and the hours. For {{ex.1.in.load_w|int}} W over {{ex.1.in.hours|int}} hours a day the cheapest is {{ex.1.out.cheapest|raw}} ({{ex.1.out.cheapest_total|rs}} over {{ex.1.out.years|int}} years); hybrid solar still has to buy a whole lithium pack and an inverter however small the load. Enter your own load and hours above.

A petrol generator runs its engine for every hour of backup, and even lightly loaded it burns a large share of its full-load fuel. At {{out.fuel_price|rs2}} a litre that is {{out.fuel_year|rs}} a year here, plus {{out.oil_year|rs}} of engine oil at one change every {{out.oil_change_hours|int}} running hours. Our fuel curve is fitted to inverter generators, so an open-frame set burns somewhat more and costs more than shown.

A UPS only pays for the units it takes back from the grid, which are more than it delivers because of charger and inverter losses: {{out.recharge_kwh_year|int}} units, {{out.ups_run_year|rs}} a year. Its real cost is the batteries, replaced every {{out.tubular_life_years|int}} years. Its charger must also refill the batteries between cuts: the calculator checks this with a {{out.charger_a|int}} A charger and leaves a UPS that cannot keep up out of the cheapest, which happens with big loads or very long cuts.

sections.h2: What the hybrid solar figure includes
p: The smallest hybrid inverter in our price data that carries the load and is built for the lithium pack's battery voltage, lithium batteries in whole packs for one night's backup, and enough panels to refill the battery on an average day in your city. It assumes the sun recharges the battery, so a run of cloudy days would still need the grid.

It does not count the bill savings solar makes during the day. The Home Power Planner on our home page does: it prices the same backup with on-grid or hybrid solar for your whole appliance list and its bill, so its pick can differ from the one here. It also leaves out mounting, cabling and installation (they add to every option, most to solar), the inverter's own standby draw and grid charging on cloudy days.

Every figure is the middle of a price range from Pakistani retailer listings or our solar price tracker, equipment only, each listed under Sources with its publisher. Retailer prices for the same model differ a lot, so replace them with your own quotes before you decide.
Battery lives are planning values: tubular {{out.tubular_life_years|int}} years and lithium {{out.lifepo4_life_years|int}} years. Heat, deep discharges and poor charging shorten both.

mistakes: Comparing purchase prices only. The cheapest option to buy is often the dearest to own; compare the cost per backup hour over the same years.
Forgetting battery replacements. A tubular bank is replaced every few years, and over the years the replacements can cost more than the UPS itself.
Sizing the comparison on the whole house. Backup usually runs fans, lights and a few appliances; enter only what runs during a cut.
Treating the solar total as a backup cost alone. Hybrid solar also cuts the day bill, which this comparison leaves out; installation and standby losses, also left out, work the other way.
safety: A generator needs a proper changeover switch so it can never feed the grid, and must run outdoors away from windows; a UPS or hybrid inverter connects to the house wiring at mains voltage. Have a licensed electrician fit the changeover, the inverter and the earthing for whichever option you choose.

faq.q: Which is cheaper for loadshedding: UPS, solar or generator?
faq.a: It depends on the load and the hours. For {{in.load_w|int}} W through {{in.hours|int}} hours a day over {{in.years|int}} years, {{out.cheapest|raw}} is cheapest at {{out.cheapest_per_hour|rs}} per backup hour; for {{ex.1.in.load_w|int}} W through {{ex.1.in.hours|int}} hours the cheapest is {{ex.1.out.cheapest|raw}} at {{ex.1.out.cheapest_per_hour|rs}}.

faq.q: How much does a petrol generator cost per hour?
faq.a: For {{in.load_w|int}} W on a {{out.gen_kva}} kVA set, about {{out.l_per_h|2}} litres an hour, {{out.fuel_year|rs}} of petrol a year at {{in.hours|int}} hours a day, plus oil. With the purchase spread over {{in.years|int}} years that is {{out.gen_per_hour|rs}} per backup hour.

faq.q: How much does it cost to recharge a UPS battery?
faq.a: The units a UPS takes from the grid are its backup units divided by the charger and inverter efficiencies: {{out.recharge_kwh_year|int}} units a year for the default load, {{out.ups_run_year|rs}} at {{out.tariff|rs2}} a unit.

faq.q: How long do UPS batteries last in Pakistan?
faq.a: Tubular batteries usually last two to five years in Pakistani heat; this calculator uses {{out.tubular_life_years|int}} years. Lithium (LiFePO4) packs are rated for thousands of cycles; it uses {{out.lifepo4_life_years|int}} years.

faq.q: Is solar worth it only for backup?
faq.a: It depends on the load and the hours. For {{ex.1.in.load_w|int}} W through {{ex.1.in.hours|int}} hours a day the cheapest backup is {{ex.1.out.cheapest|raw}}, because even a small solar backup buys a whole lithium pack and a hybrid inverter; for {{in.load_w|int}} W through {{in.hours|int}} hours over {{in.years|int}} years it is {{out.cheapest|raw}}. This comparison leaves out the bill savings solar makes during the day; the Home Power Planner on our home page counts them for your whole appliance list.
No. All three use equipment prices only. Installation, wiring and a changeover switch add to each, most to solar.
